However, in 2012, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) issued a report (GAO Report) that found that federal financial liter- acy efforts lacked meaningful coordination with multiple programs with similar goals and activities.2 Furthermore, very few federal agencies appear to monitor the effec- tiveness of their programs and only a handful of these programs have been formally assessed or evaluated for impact. Executive summary Building personal financial capability early in life can give people a foundation for later-life financial well-being. Schools are an important channel to provide the education that can improve financial capability. Financial educators and policymakers face many decisions about whether and how to implement financial education. Strong research can provide some grounding for these decisions. This report, "A review of youth financial education: Effects and evidence" responds to the question: "What evidence has been established that can guide efforts to provide young people with effective financial education?" This report reviews current research and reporting in the field, and is intended to inform policymakers, practitioners, financial educators, and researchers of the current state of rigorous evidence on financial education in schools. This report features studies that (1) evaluate youth financial education programs in schools, (2) have a causal interpretation evidenced by a randomized controlled trial, natural experiment setting, or a valid pre-post study design, and (3) have been published in peer-reviewed academic journals or as reviewed working papers. Note that the studies predominately relate to school- based programs, as this is the context in which most youth financial education research has occurred. There are three clear and consistent takeaways from the rigorous studies featured: Well-implemented state financial education mandates led to a clear improvement in financial behaviors. Many U.S. financial education programs improve financial knowledge for students, though effect sizes vary based on the population served, amount of instruction time, and topics covered. Other countries have used more widespread randomized controlled trials to study the effects of programs as they embed and expand them broadly. Treasury-related guidance and funding criteria emphasize youth financial education through a combination of policy statements, coordinated federal efforts, and explicit program recommendations. The most directly relevant Treasury page is the Financial Literacy and Education Commission (FLEC) page, which states that the Commission is chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury and coordinates efforts across 24 federal agencies to improve financial education and empower Americans to make informed financial decisions [N1-F1]. It also notes that the Commission’s mission is to set strategic direction for policy, education, practice, research, and coordination so that all Americans can make informed financial decisions, and that it serves as a partner in public and private sector efforts to improve financial knowledge, skills, and decision-making [N1-F1]. This makes Treasury itself a central institutional sponsor of youth financial education, not merely an external observer.

On specific documents, the Treasury page points to the FLEC Annual Reports to Congress, including the Strategy for Assuring Financial Empowerment (SAFE) Report, and notes that the 2025 report highlights the relevant activities of agencies represented on the FLEC to advance financial literacy and education [N1-F1]. It also references the National Strategy for Financial Literacy 2020, which underscores the federal government’s financial literacy priorities and collaboration with state, local, and tribal governments and the private sector to strengthen financial capability [N1-F1]. These documents show Treasury’s emphasis on a coordinated, multi-agency strategy rather than isolated programs.

The Treasury-supported guidance and funding criteria also emphasize broader standards and delivery expectations. In a 2019 Treasury report, the Department recommended that the FLEC designate the Money Smart curriculum and the Your Money, Your Goals program as the core resources for use by federal agencies and other partners [N2-F2]. This is a strong signal that Treasury does not just fund any program; it favors curricula that are already vetted and recognized as core resources. The same report also states that financial literacy efforts should be coordinated, and that the FLEC was established to improve financial literacy and education through a national strategy [N2-F2]. It further notes that federal agencies should evaluate for impact and that the field historically lacked meaningful coordination and effective monitoring of program effectiveness [N2-F2].

Treasury-related policy statements also point to the importance of financial empowerment as a broader goal. The FLEC page explains that the Commission’s vision is sustained financial well-being for all individuals and families, and that its strategic focus is to coordinate, support, and encourage federal government efforts to improve financial literacy and education [N1-F1]. This means youth financial education is positioned not as a narrow subject matter, but as part of a larger financial empowerment agenda that includes access to financial products and services, credit, savings, retirement, and other related capabilities [N2-F2]. Treasury thus emphasizes youth financial education as a tool for building long-term financial capability, not just knowledge.

For eligibility, delivery, and evaluation requirements, the Treasury materials are explicit but not fully prescriptive in the sense of a single program eligibility rulebook. The 2019 Treasury report recommends that programs should be actionable, relevant, and timely; improve key financial skills; build on motivation; make it easy to make good decisions and follow through; develop standards for professional educators; provide ongoing support; and evaluate for impact [N2-F2]. It also notes that the federal government spends an estimated $273 million annually on financial literacy and education programs across 23 federal agencies and entities, and that many programs lack effective monitoring and formal assessment [N2-F2]. This implies that Treasury expects funded and supported programs to demonstrate impact, but the evidence provided here does not give a detailed eligibility checklist beyond the general guidance on evaluation, coordination, and delivery standards [N2-F2].

Overall, the Treasury guidance emphasizes youth financial education through coordinated federal strategy, use of core curricula, financial empowerment as a broader goal, and explicit requirements to evaluate impact and improve delivery. The clearest documents are the FLEC page, the SAFE reports, the National Strategy for Financial Literacy 2020, and the 2019 Treasury report on coordinating and improving financial literacy efforts [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Successful youth financial education programs are associated with several key design features, many of which are supported by both the literature review and general financial literacy definitions. First, curriculum alignment with developmental and age-appropriate learning is a central theme. The literature review explicitly notes that school-based programs are an important channel for providing the education that can improve financial capability, and that many U.S. financial education programs improve financial knowledge for students, though effect sizes vary by population, instruction time, and topics covered [N3-F3]. This means the curriculum should match the developmental stage and learning needs of the audience, rather than simply covering content in a one-size-fits-all manner. The literature review also states that well-implemented state financial education mandates led to a clear improvement in financial behaviors, reinforcing that curriculum design should be tied to real-world skills and outcomes [N3-F3].

The Treasury-supported 2019 report recommends that programs should provide actionable, relevant, and timely information, improve key financial skills, build on motivation, make it easy to make good decisions and follow through, and develop standards for professional educators [N2-F2]. Third, opportunities for practice and reinforcement are repeatedly linked to effectiveness. The Treasury report stresses that programs should provide ongoing support, evaluate for impact, and make it easy to follow through [N2-F2].
